title: Ang 1377–1380: Farid's saloks, first half
hook: look under your own collar; dry bread and cool water
tomorrow: Farid says every heart is something precious. what, exactly?

segments.voice: Last week ended with Kabir: where there is forgiveness, there the Lord is. Now a new voice, a Sufi, and a new week.

The comments under somebody's post are already piling up, and every one is about what that person did wrong. Farid has a couplet for the people typing. In paraphrase, on ang 1378: Farid, if you're sharp of mind, don't write black marks against anyone; bow your head and look under your own collar. Farid was a Sufi, a Muslim saint of Punjab. So how did a Sufi's couplets end up in the Sikh scripture?
screen: `THE COMMENTS PILE UP.` → `LOOK UNDER YOUR OWN COLLAR.` → `HOW DID A SUFI GET HERE?`

segments.voice: Sikh tradition tells it this way. Guru Nanak, on his travels, came to the place where Farid's line of Sufi teachers lived on, and met the sheikh who kept Farid's words. Tradition says the verses traveled with the Guru from there, and in time they reached the Granth. The Granth itself doesn't tell the story. It simply gives Farid his own pages, under his own name. Then the couplets speak. Another, in paraphrase: eat your dry bread and drink cool water; don't look at someone else's buttered bread and burn with wanting. And another: if someone strikes you with fists, don't strike back; go home, and kiss their feet. Hard lines, plainly put. They read like a man talking to himself first, and that's the collar couplet at work: before Farid writes anyone else's black marks, he looks at his own. The Gurus kept his voice whole. A Muslim saint's words sit in the Sikh scripture beside the Gurus' own, read and sung with the same respect.
screen: `TRADITION: THE VERSES TRAVELED.` · `DRY BREAD, COOL WATER.` · `STRUCK? GO HOME, KISS THEIR FEET.` · `THE COLLAR FIRST.` · then, large: `FARID'S COUPLETS.`

segments.voice: If there's water near you, take one slow sip and notice how plain it is: cool, clear, enough. Hold the cup through the sit. Farid's dry bread and cool water are a picture of what's already enough.
Ang 1377. Where Farid's couplets begin: look under your own collar before marking anyone else.
Carry this: Farid's couplets, with plain bread, cool water, and your own collar first. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1618 COUNTS.` → `A WALK THROUGH THE GRANTH · 172 OF 180.` → `TOMORROW: EVERY HEART IS PRECIOUS. AS WHAT?`

howItsDone: Farid's saloks are read in the closing pages of the Granth and sung in kirtan like the Gurus' hymns; Sikhs know him as Baba Farid or Sheikh Farid, a Sufi of Punjab.

fork.setup: your group project flopped, and the chat is blaming the one kid who missed a deadline. you missed one too, a smaller one. what does Farid's collar couplet point to?
options: name your own miss first, then talk about fixing it together.
stay quiet; your miss was smaller, so it doesn't really count.
take the blame for all of it so nobody else has to feel bad.
fork.reveal: Farid looks under his own collar before writing anyone else's black marks. that isn't taking all the blame; it's starting with your own part.

his, fully; Farid says if someone wrongs you, write it down and keep the score.

chat.meaning: Farid: don't write black marks against others; bow your head and look under your own collar. Both parts can be true.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape story (the tradition of how Farid's verses reached the Gurus, told as 'tradition says'; the Granth itself doesn't tell it). Unity: a Muslim Sufi's words in the Sikh scripture, kept whole.
